title: What a Timeline Cannot Tell Us
script: Narrator: [measured] A timeline can be useful when studying prophetic history. It helps learners see that events occurred in an order and that a period of hardship may have extended over years. Yet a neat line across a page can create false confidence.

Narrator: While designing an exhibition panel, our team found three dates for the same event. Two came from modern websites that cited no source. The third came from a scholarly reference, but even there the author explained that the exact year was uncertain.

Narrator: [carefully] We had a choice: select one date because it looked tidy, or display the uncertainty. We chose a range and added a short note about the evidence. The panel became slightly less simple and much more honest.

Narrator: Another problem concerned sequence. A popular illustrated book placed two episodes together, making them appear to happen on consecutive days. The primary religious texts did not state that. We separated the episodes and removed the invented bridge.

Narrator: [reflective] This did not make the exhibition empty. We focused on what the sources clearly supported: the moral challenge, the response commanded by Allah, and the lessons scholars responsibly drew from the account.
Narrator: We also avoided drawing images of prophets or producing dramatic first-person voices for them. A narrator guided visitors through the evidence without pretending to recreate sacred figures.

Narrator: [thoughtful] At the exit, learners could compare “established,” “reported with disagreement,” and “not established” examples. Many said the uncertainty labels increased their trust rather than weakening the story.

Narrator: A timeline can organise information, but it cannot turn an unknown date into a fact. Responsible teaching makes room for both conviction in what revelation establishes and humility about details it does not give us.
